topic.en: What the text is about: how satellite and airborne survey changed archaeological prospection and what it still cannot do.
topic.kk: Мәтін не туралы: спутниктік және әуелік түсірілім археологиялық барлауды қалай өзгертті және әлі нені істей алмайды.
topic.ru: О чём текст: как спутниковые и воздушные съёмки изменили археологическую разведку и что они по-прежнему не умеют.

paragraphs.text: Archaeology used to begin with a rumour: a farmer turning up pottery, a road cutting through something unexpected, a local story about a buried town. Surveying a landscape properly meant walking it, field by field, picking up what lay on the surface, and the cost of that walking set a hard limit on how much ground anyone could cover. A determined team might survey a few square kilometres in a season. The area of a country is not measured in those units. The result was a discipline that knew a great deal about a few places and almost nothing about the ground between them.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Satellites changed the arithmetic. Images that were once military and expensive are now bought by the square kilometre, or looked at free of charge in a browser, and the resolution available to a university department is better than anything a state had in the 1970s. What archaeologists look for is rarely the wall itself, which is usually buried. They look for the consequences of a wall: a line of grass that dries out faster than its neighbours because the soil above the stone is thin, or a strip that stays greener over a filled ditch that holds water. Both marks are a few centimetres of difference in a growing crop, visible from six hundred kilometres up and invisible from the gate of the field.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: These marks are seasonal and unreliable. A crop mark appears in the weeks before harvest in a dry year and is invisible in a wet one, which is why the archive matters as much as the newest image. Some of the most productive work is done on photographs taken decades ago, before a site was ploughed flat or built over, and a number of projects have been assembled entirely from declassified imagery flown in the 1960s and 1970s, when much of the Middle East had not yet been irrigated or developed. Those frames were shot for other purposes entirely, which is a reminder that the most useful archive is rarely the one built for the question.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Other sensors see what the eye cannot. Instruments that measure infrared reflectance distinguish stressed vegetation before any change is visible in colour. Radar penetrates a few metres of very dry sand, which is how river channels buried beneath the Sahara were mapped. And laser scanning from aircraft, which measures the ground surface through gaps in the leaves, has done for forested landscapes what photography did for fields: complete plans of settlements under the canopy of Central America and northern Europe, produced in weeks rather than decades. Each instrument answers a different question, and a survey that uses one of them will miss what the others would have found.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The volume of data is now the constraint. A single scan of a valley produces more anomalies than a team can visit, and the great majority of them are not archaeological: a modern drain, a bomb crater, a place where a tractor turned. Machine learning has been trained on known sites to sort the candidates, and it does reduce the pile, but the published tests are honest about the limits. Models trained in one landscape perform poorly in another, and a model that has never seen a particular kind of monument will not find it. The useful role, for now, is ranking candidates for a human to look at rather than deciding which of them are real.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: None of this removes the need to dig. Imagery gives the plan of a site and almost nothing about its date, and a settlement that looks like one town from orbit may be three towns built on the same spot eight hundred years apart. Excavation remains the only way to answer when, and often the only way to answer what happened. What the surveys have changed is where the spade goes: teams now arrive with a map of the whole landscape rather than a hunch, and can choose a trench that tests a question.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: There is a second use that was not the point at the start. Because the imagery is repeated, it shows change, and much of the change is destruction: looting pits appearing across a cemetery month by month, a mound shrinking as it is quarried for soil, a site vanishing under a new suburb. Several monitoring projects now publish damage assessments that are used in court and in insurance claims. It is an uncomfortable kind of progress. The same pictures that find sites also record, with dates, how quickly they are being lost.
paragraphs.label: G
